# Board Geometry

**Status:** canonical. Changing anything here requires an ADR (see
[adr-002](adr/adr-002-coordinate-system.md)).

Derived by inspection of the 2017 physical board (photographs on the MAP 2001
poster, `FLIPHEX.pdf`). Where the poster's *prose* and the *photographs*
disagree, the photographs win — the author has stated the rules text is out of
date.

## Shape

The board is a honeycomb of **flat-top** hexagonal sockets arranged in **five
vertical columns of five cells**, with the odd columns (B and D) pushed down by
half a cell. This is the "5-row zigzag" of the roadmap seen the other way
round: the zigzag runs along the top and bottom edges, which step up-down-up.

Columns are labelled **A–E** left to right, rows **1–5** top to bottom, so every
cell has a two-character name from `A1` to `E5`. 5 x 5 = **25 cells**, matching
the 25 pieces exactly — the board fills completely and the game lasts exactly
25 plies.

```
(A1)      (C1)      (E1)
     (B1)      (D1)     
(A2)      (C2)      (E2)
     (B2)      (D2)     
(A3)      (C3)      (E3)
     (B3)      (D3)     
(A4)      (C4)      (E4)
     (B4)      (D4)     
(A5)      (C5)      (E5)
     (B5)      (D5)     
```

Odd columns are drawn indented to show the half-cell drop.

## Coordinate systems

Two representations, one canonical:

- **Offset (odd-q)** — `(col, row)`, rendered `A1`..`E5`. Human-facing: used in
  notation, logs, the CLI, and every document. Nice for humans, awkward for
  arithmetic because neighbour offsets depend on column parity.
- **Axial** `(q, r)` — canonical *inside the engine*. Neighbour arithmetic is a
  parity-free constant offset per direction, which is what makes the flip rule
  a six-element loop instead of a case analysis.

Conversion (odd-q, flat-top):

```
q = col
r = row - (col - (col & 1)) // 2
```

## Directions

Flat-top hexagons have an edge facing each of six compass directions. Arrow
slot `i` of a piece points at direction `i`, indexed **clockwise from North**:

| slot | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| direction | N | NE | SE | S | SW | NW |
| axial delta | (0,-1) | (+1,-1) | (+1,0) | (0,+1) | (-1,+1) | (-1,0) |

A rotation of `k` turns the piece `k * 60` degrees **clockwise**, mapping slot
`i` to slot `(i + k) mod 6`. Opposite directions differ by 3, which is the
identity the symmetry check below relies on.

## Adjacency

Entry *(cell, direction)* is the cell that an arrow in that slot points at, or
"—" if it points off the board. This table **is** the flip rule's lookup: when a
piece is placed on cell `X` with rotation `k`, for each arrow slot `i` of its
pattern, the affected neighbour is `adjacency[X][(i + k) mod 6]`.

| Cell | axial (q,r) | N | NE | SE | S | SW | NW | deg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A1** | (0,0) | — | — | B1 | A2 | — | — | 2 |
| **B1** | (1,0) | — | C1 | C2 | B2 | A2 | A1 | 5 |
| **C1** | (2,-1) | — | — | D1 | C2 | B1 | — | 3 |
| **D1** | (3,-1) | — | E1 | E2 | D2 | C2 | C1 | 5 |
| **E1** | (4,-2) | — | — | — | E2 | D1 | — | 2 |
| **A2** | (0,1) | A1 | B1 | B2 | A3 | — | — | 4 |
| **B2** | (1,1) | B1 | C2 | C3 | B3 | A3 | A2 | 6 |
| **C2** | (2,0) | C1 | D1 | D2 | C3 | B2 | B1 | 6 |
| **D2** | (3,0) | D1 | E2 | E3 | D3 | C3 | C2 | 6 |
| **E2** | (4,-1) | E1 | — | — | E3 | D2 | D1 | 4 |
| **A3** | (0,2) | A2 | B2 | B3 | A4 | — | — | 4 |
| **B3** | (1,2) | B2 | C3 | C4 | B4 | A4 | A3 | 6 |
| **C3** | (2,1) | C2 | D2 | D3 | C4 | B3 | B2 | 6 |
| **D3** | (3,1) | D2 | E3 | E4 | D4 | C4 | C3 | 6 |
| **E3** | (4,0) | E2 | — | — | E4 | D3 | D2 | 4 |
| **A4** | (0,3) | A3 | B3 | B4 | A5 | — | — | 4 |
| **B4** | (1,3) | B3 | C4 | C5 | B5 | A5 | A4 | 6 |
| **C4** | (2,2) | C3 | D3 | D4 | C5 | B4 | B3 | 6 |
| **D4** | (3,2) | D3 | E4 | E5 | D5 | C5 | C4 | 6 |
| **E4** | (4,1) | E3 | — | — | E5 | D4 | D3 | 4 |
| **A5** | (0,4) | A4 | B4 | B5 | — | — | — | 3 |
| **B5** | (1,4) | B4 | C5 | — | — | — | A5 | 3 |
| **C5** | (2,3) | C4 | D4 | D5 | — | B5 | B4 | 5 |
| **D5** | (3,3) | D4 | E5 | — | — | — | C5 | 3 |
| **E5** | (4,2) | E4 | — | — | — | D5 | D4 | 3 |

Verified by `gen_board_geometry.check_symmetry()`: `X` neighbours `Y` in
direction `d` if and only if `Y` neighbours `X` in direction `d + 3`.

## Structural properties

- **56 adjacent pairs** of cells.
- Degree histogram: `{2: 2, 3: 5, 4: 6, 5: 3, 6: 9}` — cells by neighbour count.
- Only **9 of 25 cells are interior** (degree 6). The board is mostly edge, so
  border effects dominate; a piece's realised power is far below its arrow
  count on most cells. This should show up in Phase 6's branching analysis and
  is a candidate move-ordering signal for the Phase 3 solver.
- The two degree-2 cells are `A1` and `E1`, the poorest cells on the board.

### The board is not centrally symmetric — and that matters

Columns A, C, E carry cells at vertical offsets 0..4 while B and D sit at
0.5..4.5. Those two sets of columns have different vertical centres (2 and
2.5), so no rotation or reflection maps the cell set onto itself: the board's
symmetry group is **trivial**. The shape "leans". Concretely `C1` has degree 3
while `C5` has degree 5, and `A1`/`E1` (degree 2) have no degree-2 partners
under any candidate symmetry.

This is a real asymmetry in the physical artifact, not a modelling artifact,
and it is directly relevant to **H1 (first-player advantage)**: on a board with
no symmetry group, there is no strategy-stealing or pairing argument available,
so H1 has to be settled computationally. Worth stating explicitly in the
writeup — it is part of why the game is interesting.

> **OPEN-1.** Confirm against the physical board that all five columns really
> hold five cells and that no cell is missing from a corner. The poster
> photograph is consistent with 5x5=25 and with the 25-piece count, but it is a
> low-resolution photograph taken at an angle.
